LESSON MENU
THEORY OF OPERATION
Most motors are required to deliver a constant output RPM, regardless of shaft load.
DISCUSSION
A loaded DC motor exhibits a reduced output of RPM.
A loaded motor produces more torque and less CEMF..........
To maintain a steady output RPM, the loaded DC motor must have an increased input voltage.
If the load decreases, the input voltage must be reduced to keep the RPM constant.
In other words, a changing load on a DC motor requires a changing input voltage to keep RPM constant.
How is a changing input voltage sent to the motor?
One method is to use a time control circuit................
This requires you to adjust the circuit as the load changes.
The process is simple for human control and is called a feedback system.
The block diagram shows a typical human feedback system....
A tachometer might be used to display motor RPM. nsor (Tachometer)
You could then decide if the motor RPM is correct, too slow, or too fast.
If the motor's RPM is too slow or too fast, adjustments to the speed control circuit are made.
The changed voltage output of the speed control circuit causes the motors RPM to change.
Consequently, the sensor indicates a different RPM and you observe the results and make additional adjustments if necessary.
The process continues until the motor is turned off.
The system is a feedback system since the output from the motor has an effect on its input.
This system is inefficient since a person is needed to make the feedback system work.
A complete electronic feedback control circuit is much more desirable.
In the "human operator" feedback circuit, the operator receives direct input from _______
The motor's output signal is received by the operator indirectly.
TRY AGAIN!
The speed control circuitry receives an input from the operator.
TRY AGAIN!
An electronic feedback system eliminates the human, but still operates the same.
An electronic comparator is used in place of a human operator.
The comparator "compares" the feedback signal from the motor to some predetermined base motor speed.
If the feedback signal is larger than the base speed signal, the comparator sends a negative signal to the motor drive circuit.
This negative signal tells the motor drive circuit to reduce the input signal to the motor, slowing the motor down.
If the feedback signal is smaller than the base speed signal, the comparator sends a positive signal to the motor drive circuit.
This positive signal tells the motor drive circuit to increase the input signal to the motor, speeding the motor up.

1. Feedback circuits are designed to maintain a constant DC motor RPM regardless of motor shaft load.
2. Feedback circuits utilize the motors output to determine the input voltage to the motor.
3. A human controlled feedback system utilizes a person making decisions.
4. An electronic feedback system incorporates an electronic comparator in place of a human operator.
5. The comparator "compares" the motor's feedback signal to a predetermined base motor speed.
6. The comparator sends a "weighted" signal to the motor drive circuit.
7. The motor drive circuit controls the input signal to the DC motor.
